model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my geography teacher. I had her when I was about fifteen, until I finished school.

Before her, geography was boring subject for me. It was only capitals and rivers and mountains, and we must learn all of them by heart. I was not good at it and I didn't like it, so I was always sitting at the back.

But she taught us in a different way. In her first lesson she asked us why one street in our town is flooding every year in autumn. Nobody knew the answer. So we go outside and we look at the road and the drains, and after that she explained it to us. And after that every topic was a question, not a list.

So my opinion about geography changed a lot. Now I think geography is not memorising, it is explaining why the things are where they are. Also my marks were better, from C to A, and I felt very happy about this. She was a very good teacher and I will never forget her. So this is the teacher who changed how I think about a subject.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
I'd like to talk about my geography teacher — I had her for two years, from about fifteen, and she completely changed what I thought the subject was for.

Up until then, geography had been the subject I was worst at. It was basically a list to be learned — capitals, rivers, the heights of mountains — and I'd never once been asked why any of it was there. I'd more or less written myself off as someone who wasn't a geography person, which at fifteen feels permanent.

What she did differently was start with a question we actually cared about. In her very first lesson she asked us why one particular street in our town flooded every autumn, and none of us had the faintest idea. Instead of telling us, she walked us down there to look at it — the slope of the road, where the drains were, what had been built above it. By the end of the afternoon we'd worked most of it out ourselves, and I remember being slightly annoyed that it had been that simple all along.

As for how my view changed, I stopped seeing geography as something to memorise and started seeing it as a way of accounting for why things end up where they do. My marks went up, which was nice, but that isn't really the point. The point is that she showed me the difference between knowing a fact and being able to explain it, and that's stayed with me in every subject since.

'Written myself off', 'the faintest idea', 'accounting for' replace the band-6 adjectives.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
This is about the teacher who more or less rescued geography for me. I had her from around fifteen, for the last two years of school.

Before she arrived the subject had been a memory test and nothing else — capitals, rivers, the occasional diagram of a valley, all of it to be swallowed whole and handed back in an exam. I'd quietly filed myself under 'not a geography person', which at that age feels like a fact about you rather than a decision you've made.

Her first lesson was a single question: why did one street in the town flood every autumn when the road two hundred metres further up the hill never did? Not one of us could say. What she resisted, and I only appreciate this now, was the urge to tell us. She walked us down there instead and let us stand about looking at drains until somebody noticed the new car park at the top of the slope. It took the best part of an hour to arrive at something she could have said in thirty seconds.

Only later did I work out what she'd actually been teaching. It wasn't the flooding at all — it was that a fact you've assembled yourself behaves quite differently from one you've been handed. My marks improved, though that's the least interesting part of it. What she left me with was a habit: whenever something is where it is, ask what put it there. And that, I'd say, is the difference between a subject you've sat through and one you've genuinely learned.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion after 'only later' where band 7 used a plain past simple.
'Swallowed whole', 'the best part of an hour', 'filed myself under' sit naturally, not on display.
The close abstracts into a claim about learning rather than summarising the story.

annotations.label: Inversion after a fronted adverbial
annotations.why: One inversion per long turn lifts the register without sounding written.

annotations.span: all of it to be swallowed whole and handed back in an exam

annotations.why: One vivid image beats four abstract nouns about rote learning.

annotations.span: What she resisted, and I only appreciate this now, was the urge to tell us.

model_answers.transcript:
I would like to talk about chemistry. I studied it in secondary school, from fourteen years old until sixteen.

We had chemistry two times in a week, and one of them was a double lesson on Thursday afternoon in the laboratory. I liked this lesson very much. In other subjects the teacher is talking and we are writing, but in chemistry we are doing things with our hands.

The thing I remember most is the experiment where you put drops of one liquid into another one, and you must stop exactly when the colour is changing. It is very difficult. The first time I put too much and I must start again. But after four or five times I did it correct, and I was very happy.

Why I enjoyed it, I think it is because you know immediately if you are right or wrong. In history you write an essay and then you wait two weeks for the mark. In chemistry the colour changes or it doesn't change. Also the laboratory was very quiet and I felt very calm there. So chemistry was my favourite subject at school.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The subject I'd pick is chemistry. I did it from about fourteen through to sixteen, and it was easily the part of the week I looked forward to most.

We had it twice a week, but the one that mattered was a double period on Thursday afternoons, down in the lab. That was the whole appeal, really. Even getting there felt different — you went down a back staircase and the whole corridor smelled faintly of gas taps. In almost every other subject somebody talked at the front and you copied it down; in chemistry you actually had something in your hands for eighty minutes.

The lessons I remember best were the titrations. Essentially you add one liquid into another drop by drop and you have to stop at the exact moment the colour turns. My first attempt went straight past the point and I had to start the whole thing again, and it took four or five goes before I could do it reliably. Nobody told you when to stop, either; you had to watch for it yourself and commit. It was pure trial and error, but that was half the appeal.

The reason I enjoyed it, if I'm honest, came down to feedback. In history you hand in an essay and wait a fortnight to find out what you'd misunderstood; in the lab the colour either changed or it didn't, and you knew within a second. There was also something oddly calming about the room — thirty people all concentrating and nobody saying much. I've never really found that combination anywhere since.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
If I had to pick one it would be chemistry. I took it from fourteen until I left school at sixteen, and Thursday afternoon was the one slot on the timetable I'd never have given up.

Two lessons a week, and the second was a double period down in the lab, which is where the whole thing lived for me. Most subjects at that age consisted of one person talking and thirty people transcribing. Chemistry was the only one where you spent eighty minutes with your hands busy, and where being wrong was information rather than embarrassment.

What I remember best are the titrations. You let one liquid into another a drop at a time, and the entire exercise turns on stopping at precisely the instant the colour goes. My first attempt sailed straight past it, and it took four or five goes before I could catch it reliably. Tedious, on paper. In practice it was the nearest thing school ever offered to a game.

Looking back, what I was enjoying wasn't chemistry as such — it was the speed of the feedback. Hand in a history essay and you wait a fortnight to discover what you'd got wrong; in the lab the answer arrived inside a second and owed nothing to anybody's opinion. Very little I've done since has been that honest with me that quickly, and I suspect that is what people are really describing when they say a subject suited them.

'Sailed straight past it', 'information rather than embarrassment' — precision, not display.

annotations.span: sailed straight past it
annotations.label: Idiom sitting where it belongs
annotations.why: Use it for overshooting anything — a target, a deadline, a turning.

annotations.span: Tedious, on paper. In practice it was the nearest thing school ever offered to a game.

annotations.why: A very short sentence between two long ones is a genuine spoken rhythm.

annotations.span: Hand in a history essay and you wait a fortnight to discover what you'd got wrong
annotations.label: Imperative used as a conditional
annotations.why: 'Do X and Y happens' is a spoken alternative to 'if' — vary the pattern.

annotations.span: what people are really describing when they say a subject suited them
annotations.label: Closes above the anecdote
annotations.why: Turn the last line into a claim about people, not about you.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about driving. I learned to drive when I was twenty-four, and I thought it will take three months, but in the end it took more than one year.

At the beginning it was okay. The instructor is very patient and we practise in a quiet area near my house, so there was no traffic. But the problem was the clutch. Every time I stopped on a hill, the engine is stopping, and I feel very stupid because there are cars behind me. I did this maybe forty times.

And also I failed my first test. On the roundabout I didn't see a motorbike, so the examiner stopped the test immediately. I was very disappointed and I didn't drive again for two months.

Then my brother said we must practise the same road every evening. So we did this for six weeks, the same twenty minutes every day, and slowly it became easy. And after that I passed the second test.

So it took me fourteen months and not three months. I learned that some things are needing more time. This is the skill which took longer than I expected.

Five sentences begin with 'so' or 'and', so the sequence has no visible shape.
'Okay', 'stupid', 'disappointed', 'easy' — every judgement is a single flat adjective.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The skill I'd go for is driving. I learned at twenty-four, which is late where I'm from, and I'd assumed the whole thing would take about three months. In the end it took fourteen.

The early lessons were fine. My instructor was extremely patient, and we spent the first month going round a quiet industrial estate near my flat where there was genuinely nothing to hit. What caught me out was hill starts. There's a particular junction on a slope near the station, and I must have stalled there thirty or forty times — clutch up too fast, engine dead, queue building behind me. Every time it happened I got a little tighter about the next one, which of course made the next one worse.

By about month eight I'd more or less convinced myself I was never going to manage it. Then I failed my first test. I pulled onto a roundabout without checking properly, and there was a motorbike coming that I simply hadn't seen. The examiner ended it there and then. I didn't get back into a car for about two months afterwards, which I now think was the real mistake.

What finally worked was my brother's idea, and it was completely unglamorous: the same twenty-minute route, every evening, for six weeks. Same junction, same roundabout, same order. By the end of it I wasn't thinking about the clutch at all — my feet were just doing it while I looked at the road. I passed second time, and honestly the thing I took from it wasn't about driving — it was that repetition does the work that motivation gets the credit for.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
Driving, without much hesitation. I came to it at twenty-four, which where I grew up is embarrassingly late, and I had it in my head that three months would cover it. Fourteen, as it turned out.

The first stretch was painless enough — a month circling an empty industrial estate with an instructor who never once raised his voice. Hill starts were where it fell apart. There is a junction on a slope by the station that I must have stalled on thirty or forty times, and the trouble with stalling is that it is entirely public: the engine dies, a queue forms behind you, and every subsequent attempt carries the weight of the last one.

Then I failed the test outright — pulled onto a roundabout, missed a motorbike I had no business missing, and that was that. What I did next was the genuine error. I stayed out of a car for two months and told myself I was letting my nerves settle, when what I was actually doing was avoiding the thing altogether.

What eventually shifted it was my brother's suggestion, and there was nothing clever about it: the same twenty-minute loop, every evening, for six weeks. Same junction, same roundabout, same order, until none of it required deciding any more. Had I done that from the outset I would have passed inside six months. Which is the part worth keeping, I suppose — we tend to credit motivation with results that repetition has quietly produced.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces the third conditional, and a colon carries a three-clause explanation.
'No business missing', 'that was that', 'entirely public' are exact, not decorative.

My goal was to change to design work. But for this you need a portfolio with your projects, and I had nothing at all. So I decided I will make six projects in one year.

model_answers.transcript:
The goal I'll talk about is one I set myself about three years ago, and it took eleven months to finish.

At the time I was working in the admin department of an insurance company. It was a perfectly decent job and I was quietly miserable in it. What I actually wanted was to move into design, and the obstacle was completely practical: nobody will interview you without a portfolio, and I didn't have a single finished piece to show anyone.

So I set myself a target — six real projects in twelve months. Not exercises, not briefs I'd invented for myself; six jobs somebody had genuinely asked for. I gave it Tuesday and Thursday evenings and Sunday mornings, and the first three I did for nothing: a menu for a friend's café, a leaflet for a small charity, and a poster for a band my brother knew. Working for free opened doors that an application never would have.

The honest part is that around month five I very nearly stopped. I was tired the whole time, the fourth job was going badly, and I remember deciding that people who finished things like this were simply built differently from me. What kept me at it was that I'd told far too many people about it to back out quietly.

I finished in eleven months, applied for three jobs and got one of them. Looking back, what I'd underestimated wasn't the work — it was how long you have to keep going after the excitement wears off.

model_answers.transcript:
The goal was a portfolio, and it took me eleven months rather than the twelve I'd allowed myself.

I was on the admin side of an insurance company at the time — a job I had no complaint about and no appetite for, which is a worse combination than it sounds. Design was what I wanted, and the barrier was neither talent nor money but something a great deal duller: nobody will look at you without a body of work, and a body of work is exactly what you cannot assemble until somebody looks at you.

So the target was six commissioned pieces in a year. Commissioned mattered. Not practice, not invented briefs — six things a real person had asked for and intended to use. Tuesday and Thursday evenings, Sunday mornings, and the first three done for nothing: a café menu, a charity leaflet, a poster for a band. Working free bought me the one thing an application never does, which is somebody's actual opinion.

Month five was when it nearly ended, and not dramatically. I simply stopped believing I was the sort of person who finishes things. What carried me through was rather less admirable than persistence — I had told far too many people to be able to drop it quietly.

I'll describe a group project from my second year at university. The four of us had three weeks to produce a report on independent cafés in the city, and it very nearly didn't happen.

I knew two of the others reasonably well; the fourth was somebody I'd never spoken to before that term. In the first meeting we split it up sensibly enough — I took the interviews, one of the others took the figures, and we agreed a date for each section.

The problem started about ten days in. One member simply went quiet. He wasn't answering messages, he didn't turn up to two meetings, and with a week to go we still had no idea whether his section existed at all. Chasing him up was getting us nowhere, and by then we were all fairly close to panicking.

What actually solved it was embarrassingly simple. We set up a shared document where every section was listed with a name against it and a date, so anybody could see at a glance what was finished and what wasn't. On top of that we had a twenty-minute call every Wednesday evening — no agenda, just each of us saying where we'd got to.

We redistributed his part between the three of us and handed it in on time. It got a good mark, though that isn't really the bit I remember. What made the difference wasn't goodwill or effort; it was making the work visible, so that not doing yours became obvious rather than private.

This was a group project in my second year — four of us, three weeks, and a report on the independent cafés in the city that came within a day of never existing.

Two of the group I knew well; with the fourth I had barely exchanged a sentence. The division of labour itself was sensible and we did it properly at the first meeting: interviews to me, figures to somebody else, every section with a name and a date attached to it.

Ten days in, one of us went quiet. Not hostile, not apologetic — simply absent. No replies, two missed meetings, and with a week left none of us could say whether his share was half written or had never been started. Chasing him produced nothing beyond a growing sense that three people were about to be punished for one person's silence.

What rescued it was almost insultingly basic. Everything went into one shared document, each section headed with a name and a deadline, and we added a twenty-minute call on Wednesday evenings where each of us said out loud where we had got to. Inside two days the picture was clear enough to act on, and we split his section three ways.

It got a decent mark, which is the least interesting part of it. What I took away is that most group failures aren't failures of willingness. They're failures of visibility — people very rarely abandon work that everybody can watch them not doing.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to describe the place where I work in my home. It is in my bedroom, in the corner near the window.

There is a desk, a chair and two screens. Also there is a lamp and a box with papers under the desk. On the walls there is nothing, only white paint. The desk was from my neighbour, because she moved to another city and she didn't want to take it.

I use it every morning from nine o'clock, and on Thursday I use it the whole day, because I don't go to the office in Thursday. In the other days I go to the office by bus.

It is good for concentration because it is very quiet and nobody disturb me. But it is also not so good, because my bedroom is small, and when I finish the work I still see the desk in front of me. So I never really stop. I think if I have another room it will be better, but now it is okay.

So this is the place in my home where I work.

what_caps_it.point: The description is a list of nouns with 'there is' four times and no relative clause.
'Nobody disturb', 'in Thursday', 'if I have… it will be' — three separate patterns misfire.
The evaluation runs on 'good' and 'not so good' and then restates the card.

annotations.label: Locates it before describing it
annotations.why: Keep this — two prepositions in the first sentence orient the listener instantly.

annotations.span: There is a desk, a chair and two screens.
annotations.label: Flat list with no relationship
annotations.why: Attach one clause: 'a desk that takes up most of the corner'.

annotations.span: I don't go to the office in Thursday
annotations.label: Wrong preposition with a day
annotations.why: 'On Thursdays'. Store the preposition with the day, as one chunk.

annotations.span: nobody disturb me
annotations.label: Agreement missing after 'nobody'
annotations.why: 'Nobody disturbs me.' Indefinite pronouns are singular, always.

annotations.span: if I have another room it will be better
annotations.label: Real conditional for an unreal wish
annotations.why: 'If I had another room it'd be better' — past simple plus 'would'.

annotations.span: So this is the place in my home where I work.
annotations.label: Closes on the card's own words
annotations.why: Finish with the change you'd make, not with the prompt repeated.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The place I'd describe isn't really a room at all — it's a corner of my bedroom, under the window, facing the wall of the building next door.

There's a desk that takes up most of that corner, and it arrived more or less by accident: a neighbour was moving out and couldn't be bothered to take it with her, so I carried it up two flights of stairs and it's been there ever since. On it there are two screens and a lamp I never switch off, and underneath there's a cardboard box of paperwork I keep meaning to deal with. That's the whole thing. Nothing on the walls.

I use it every weekday morning, and on Thursdays I'm there from nine until about six, because that's the day nobody expects me in the office. The rest of the week I'm only at it for a couple of hours before I leave, so it gets the sharpest part of the day and none of the tired part.

As for whether it suits me — half of it does. It's the quietest spot in the flat and nobody comes in, so for anything that needs actual concentration it's ideal. What doesn't work is that it sits about three metres from my bed. The commute is wonderful and the shutting-off is impossible: I finish at six, turn round, and the desk is still sitting there looking at me. If I had a spare room I'd move it tomorrow. As things are, I've settled for turning the lamp off, which is a fairly feeble ritual but it's better than nothing.

what_lifts_it.point: Objects arrive inside relative clauses instead of a queue of 'there is' sentences.
Past continuous, present perfect and a second conditional all appear where they belong.
The evaluation splits into two halves, so the last bullet has a visible structure.

annotations.span: it's a corner of my bedroom, under the window, facing the wall of the building next door
annotations.label: Three positions, no list
annotations.why: Prepositions of place do the describing; adjectives are not needed at all.

annotations.span: There's a desk that takes up most of that corner
annotations.label: Existential plus relative clause
annotations.why: Never say 'there is X' twice in a row — hang a clause off the first.

annotations.span: a neighbour was moving out and couldn't be bothered to take it with her
annotations.label: Past continuous as background
annotations.why: Use the continuous for the situation and the simple for the event.

annotations.span: it's been there ever since
annotations.label: Present perfect for duration
annotations.why: Any object you own can take 'I've had it since' or 'ever since'.

annotations.span: so it gets the sharpest part of the day and none of the tired part
annotations.label: Adds a judgement to a fact
annotations.why: One evaluative clause after a plain statement stops the turn becoming a timetable.

annotations.span: That's the whole thing. Nothing on the walls.
annotations.label: Closes the description deliberately
annotations.why: Say when you have finished describing; it stops the list running on.

annotations.span: As for whether it suits me — half of it does.
annotations.label: Signposts and splits the last bullet
annotations.why: 'Half of it does' promises two parts and forces you to give both.

annotations.span: The commute is wonderful and the shutting-off is impossible
annotations.label: One sentence holds both halves
annotations.why: Balance the benefit and the cost in a single clause pair.

annotations.span: If I had a spare room I'd move it tomorrow.
annotations.label: Second conditional, correctly built
annotations.why: This is the natural structure for any 'what would you change' moment.

annotations.span: I finish at six, turn round, and the desk is still sitting there looking at me
annotations.label: Three beats, then a fall
annotations.why: Keep the first two clauses level and drop the pitch on the third.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
Calling it a workspace flatters it. It's a corner of my bedroom, under the window, with a view of somebody else's brickwork about four metres away.

The desk arrived by pure chance. A neighbour was moving out, couldn't face carrying it down, and offered it to whoever wanted it; I got it up two flights of stairs and it hasn't moved since. Two screens, a lamp that stays on whatever the hour, and a box of paperwork underneath that I've been intending to sort out for well over a year. The walls are bare, which was never a decision — I simply never got round to it.

Weekday mornings I'm there by nine, and on Thursdays I don't leave it at all, since that's the day nobody expects me anywhere else. It gets the first three hours of my attention and nothing after four, which is probably the only sensible arrangement in the whole flat.

Does it suit me? Half of it does, and the half that doesn't is the half nobody warns you about. For concentration it's unbeatable: no interruptions, no corridor conversation, nobody appearing at my shoulder. What it costs is the ending. There's no journey home to mark the day as over, and a desk three metres from your pillow is a very efficient way of never quite stopping. Were there a spare room in the flat, that desk would be in it by the weekend. Failing that, I switch the lamp off at six, which is more a gesture than a solution, though I've noticed it does help.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion replaces 'if', and a gerund subject opens the whole turn.
'Flatters it', 'more a gesture than a solution' judge without a single evaluative adjective.
A self-addressed question reopens the last bullet instead of signposting it flatly.

annotations.span: Calling it a workspace flatters it.
annotations.label: Gerund subject as an opener
annotations.why: Five words that describe and evaluate at once; no preamble required.

annotations.span: Were there a spare room in the flat, that desk would be in it by the weekend.
annotations.label: Inversion instead of 'if there were'
annotations.why: Same meaning as the second conditional, one register higher, still spoken.

annotations.span: no interruptions, no corridor conversation, nobody appearing at my shoulder
annotations.label: Three negatives in one run
annotations.why: Group them tightly and let only the last one fall.

annotations.span: a very efficient way of never quite stopping
annotations.label: Praise used to criticise
annotations.why: Calling a drawback 'efficient' is dry understatement, and examiners hear it.

annotations.span: more a gesture than a solution
annotations.label: Two nouns weighed against each other
annotations.why: Reuse it whenever you want to admit something only half works.

annotations.span: the half that doesn't is the half nobody warns you about
annotations.label: Turns the split into a claim
annotations.why: A general observation inside your own description raises the whole turn.

model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about a friend of my father. He is about fifty-five years old and he lives in the same street as my parents.

His job is he checks the bridges. He works for the government office for the roads in our region. Every week he goes to different bridges and tunnels and he looks if there is a problem. Sometimes he must go under the bridge with ropes, like a climber. He has also a small hammer, and he hits the concrete, because from the sound he can understand if the metal inside is rusty.

I know about this job because he came to my school one time to talk about it, and after that I asked him many questions.

I find it interesting because it is a job that nobody thinks about. Everybody drives on the bridge every morning and nobody knows that somebody is checking it. He told me that in thirty years he closed two bridges, and nobody said thank you, because nothing happened. It is very interesting job. So this is the person whose job I find interesting.

model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd talk about is a friend of my father's — he's in his mid-fifties and he's lived four doors down from my parents for as long as I can remember.

His job is inspecting bridges. He works for the regional roads authority, and what that means in practice is that he spends most of the week driving out to bridges and tunnels and checking whether anything has started to go wrong. Some of it is fairly dramatic: he's harnessed and lowered underneath the deck on ropes, so that he can reach the parts nobody sees from the road. Most of it is far less exciting than that. He carries a small hammer and taps the concrete, and from the sound it makes he can tell whether the steel inside has begun to corrode.

I only know any of this because he came into my school once to talk about what he did, and I pestered him about it for years afterwards. My father says he has never once heard him describe the job as boring, which after three decades strikes me as unusual.

What interests me about it is that it's a job defined entirely by things not happening. Thousands of people drive over that bridge every morning without a thought, and the whole point of his work is that they never have to have one. He's told me he's condemned two structures in thirty years, and on both occasions nobody thanked him, because nothing collapsed. There's something in that I've never quite got out of my head.

what_lifts_it.point: Present perfect for duration, a passive, a purpose clause and an embedded 'whether'.
The best idea is signposted with a cleft and then given thirty seconds, not one line.
'Pestered him', 'condemned two structures', 'corrode' are the precise words, not big ones.

annotations.label: One verb replaces a whole clause
annotations.why: 'Pestered' says asked repeatedly and slightly annoyingly, in one word.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The person I'd pick is a friend of my father's, a man in his mid-fifties who has lived four doors along from my parents for as long as I have been alive.

He inspects bridges. He's employed by the regional roads authority, and the work amounts to driving out to bridges and tunnels and establishing, structure by structure, whether anything has begun to fail. Parts of it look like something from a documentary — he's harnessed and lowered beneath the deck to reach surfaces nobody has laid eyes on since the thing was built. The rest is almost comically ordinary. He carries a small hammer, taps the concrete, and listens; a dull note where a sharp one belongs tells him the steel underneath has started to rust.

None of this would have reached me had he not come into my school one afternoon to talk about it. I pestered him for details for years afterwards, and he was patient about it in a way adults rarely are.

What draws me to it is that it's a profession defined by absence. Thousands of people cross that bridge every morning without a flicker of thought, and the entire purpose of the job is that they never need one. He's condemned two structures in thirty years and, as he puts it, nobody has ever thanked him, because on both occasions nothing whatsoever happened. That strikes me as a far more serious achievement than most of the ones people talk about.

what_lifts_it.point: Inversion carries a third conditional, and an interrupting adverbial holds the sentence open.
'Comically ordinary', 'a flicker of thought', 'defined by absence' are exact, not ornamental.
The close converts the anecdote into a claim about what achievement means.

model_answers.label: Where most candidates land
model_answers.transcript:
I want to talk about my final maths exam in the school. I did it when I was eighteen, in June, and it was very important because my university place is depending on it.

For preparing I used the old exams from the previous years. My teacher gave us maybe twelve of them and I did all of them at home, usually in the evening, two or three hours. After that I checked the answers in the back of the paper. My marks were quite good, so I felt confident.

But in the exam there was a problem. I didn't finish. There were eight questions and I answered only six, because I spent too much time in the first ones. When the teacher said five minutes I started to panic and my writing became terrible.

In the end I passed, but the mark was lower than I expect. If I do it again, I will use a clock when I practise at home. Because knowing the maths is not enough, you must also know the time. So this is the exam that I prepared very hard for.

what_caps_it.point: A stative verb goes continuous, a comparison loses its tense and the conditional is the wrong one.
'Quite good', 'terrible', 'very important' — and 'the old exams' for 'past papers'.
The best idea, separating the subject from the exam, gets one sentence and no development.

model_answers.label: The target — same story, better language
model_answers.transcript:
The exam I'll describe is the maths paper I sat at the end of school, when I was eighteen. It mattered a great deal, because the university place I'd been offered depended entirely on the grade.

The way I prepared was almost entirely past papers. My teacher handed out about a dozen of them going back years, and over roughly two months I worked through every one at the kitchen table in the evenings. I'd do a paper, mark it against the answers in the back, and note down whatever I'd got wrong. On paper it was going well — by the end of May I was scoring comfortably higher than the offer needed.

There was a fair amount riding on it, and I'd convinced myself the hard part was behind me.

The exam itself did not go to plan. There were eight questions and I only finished six, because I'd spent nearly forty minutes on the first two and never really made that time back. When the invigilator called five minutes I was halfway through question seven, and I remember my handwriting falling apart.

I passed, but a grade below what I'd been getting at home, and the reason is fairly obvious in hindsight. I hadn't timed myself once in two months. I'd rehearsed the maths and completely neglected the exam. If I were doing it again I'd put a clock on the table from the very first paper, because knowing how to answer a question and knowing how long you can afford to spend on it are two quite different skills.

what_lifts_it.point: Three past perfects and a correctly built second conditional carry the two time layers.
'Past papers', 'invigilator', 'made that time back' are the exact words for this world.
The fourth bullet gets a real change and a general principle instead of a resolution.

annotations.span: The exam I'll describe is the maths paper I sat at the end of school, when I was eighteen.
annotations.label: Names it and dates it at once
annotations.why: Exam, stage and age in one sentence. There is no need for a preamble.

annotations.span: the university place I'd been offered depended entirely on the grade
annotations.label: Past perfect passive in a relative clause
annotations.why: Use it to say what had already happened before the story begins.

annotations.span: On paper it was going well
annotations.label: Idiom that also fits the subject
annotations.why: 'On paper' means in theory — a natural way to set up a reversal.

annotations.span: The exam itself did not go to plan.
annotations.label: Marks the turn in six words
annotations.why: A short flat sentence between paragraphs is worth more than 'unfortunately'.

annotations.span: I'd spent nearly forty minutes on the first two and never really made that time back
annotations.label: Past perfect explains the outcome
annotations.why: The earlier action needs the perfect; the result stays in past simple.

annotations.span: I remember my handwriting falling apart
annotations.label: Stress lands on 'falling apart'
annotations.why: Slow the last two words slightly; the image does the emotional work.

annotations.span: the reason is fairly obvious in hindsight
annotations.label: Signals a judgement is coming
annotations.why: 'In hindsight' buys you a second and promises evaluation, not more story.

annotations.span: I hadn't timed myself once in two months.
annotations.label: Past perfect for the omission
annotations.why: Saying what you had not done is often stronger than what you did.

annotations.span: If I were doing it again I'd put a clock on the table from the very first paper
annotations.label: Answers the bullet with one change
annotations.why: One physical action, in a second conditional. Never 'I'd work harder'.

model_answers.label: The ceiling — one further step
model_answers.transcript:
The one I'd choose is the maths paper at the end of school, sat at eighteen, with a university offer hanging on the grade.

My preparation was past papers and almost nothing else. The teacher handed out a dozen or so going back years, and across two months I worked through every one of them at the kitchen table after supper — do the paper, mark it against the answers, write down what I'd got wrong. By the end of May I was scoring comfortably above what the offer asked for, and I walked in on the morning feeling something close to relaxed.

That confidence was the first thing the morning took off me.

The paper had other ideas. Eight questions; I finished six. I'd given the first two nearly forty minutes between them and never made the time back, so when the invigilator called five minutes I was somewhere in the middle of question seven with my handwriting coming apart in front of me.

I passed, a grade below everything I'd managed at home, and the diagnosis is embarrassingly simple. Not once in two months had I put a clock on the table. I'd rehearsed the mathematics and ignored the examination, which are not the same object at all. Were I doing it over, every paper would be timed from the first one onwards — because the thing being tested that morning was never really algebra. It was how to spend a hundred and twenty minutes.

what_lifts_it.point: Two inversions — after a negative adverbial and instead of 'if' — do the structural work.
'Had other ideas', 'the same object', 'something close to relaxed' are precise, not showy.
The close reframes the whole story as being about time rather than about mathematics.

annotations.span: Not once in two months had I put a clock on the table.
annotations.label: Inversion after a negative adverbial
annotations.why: Front the negative, invert the verb; it emphasises without raising your voice.

annotations.span: Were I doing it over, every paper would be timed from the first one onwards
annotations.label: Inverted second conditional
annotations.why: 'Were I' replaces 'if I were' and lifts the register in two words.

annotations.span: The paper had other ideas.
annotations.label: Four words carry the reversal
annotations.why: Give the exam a will of its own; it is faster than any adverb.

annotations.span: I'd rehearsed the mathematics and ignored the examination, which are not the same object at all
annotations.label: Two nouns separated precisely
annotations.why: Naming the distinction exactly is what the top of Lexical Resource rewards.

annotations.span: Eight questions; I finished six.
annotations.label: Two clipped groups, no linking
annotations.why: A deliberate break between them makes the shortfall audible.

annotations.span: the thing being tested that morning was never really algebra
annotations.label: Reframes the whole answer
annotations.why: Say what was really being measured and the anecdote becomes an argument.
